title: Parlour Spanish A1 Grammar Reference
description: A single concise reference covering the core grammar taught and practised in Parlour A1 Latin American Spanish.
usage: Reference content for learners. Each topic is designed to be readable independently and short enough for an in-app reference panel.
notes: Latin American Spanish is used throughout. Ustedes is used for plural you; vosotros is not included.
Regional variation exists across Latin America. This reference presents broadly standard forms suitable for a general LatAm curriculum.
The reference is intentionally concise. It explains the A1 system without attempting to cover every grammatical possibility.

topics.title: Articles
topics.explanation: Spanish uses definite articles (the) and indefinite articles (a/an, some). The article normally agrees with the noun in gender and number.
rules: el = masculine singular; la = feminine singular; los = masculine/mixed plural; las = feminine plural.
un = masculine singular; una = feminine singular; unos = masculine plural; unas = feminine plural.
Spanish normally uses an article where English may omit one, especially when talking about a general noun.
Singular agua uses el because its stressed initial a sounds like a masculine article, but agua remains feminine: el agua fría.

topics.title: Noun gender
topics.explanation: Every Spanish noun has grammatical gender. Many nouns ending in -o are masculine and many ending in -a are feminine, but there are important exceptions.
rules: Common masculine endings include -o, -ma and -pa in many words: libro, problema, mapa.
Common feminine endings include -a, -ción, -sión and -dad: casa, canción, universidad.
Gender is grammatical, so it does not always correspond to biological sex.
Learn the article with a new noun: el problema, la ciudad.

topics.title: Plural nouns
topics.explanation: Plural nouns normally take -s after a vowel and -es after a consonant. Spelling and accent changes sometimes occur.
rules: Vowel + s: casa → casas, libro → libros.
Consonant + es: papel → papeles, ciudad → ciudades.
Words ending in z change z to c before -es: luz → luces, lápiz → lápices.
Some words change their written stress when pluralised: joven → jóvenes, examen → exámenes.

topics.title: Gender and adjective agreement
topics.explanation: Adjectives normally agree with the noun they describe in gender and number.
rules: -o/-a adjectives change for gender: alto, alta.
Plural normally adds -s after a vowel: alto → altos.
Adjectives ending in -e or many consonants usually do not change for gender: grande, interesante, fácil.
The adjective usually comes after the noun, although common adjectives can sometimes come before it.

topics.title: Subject pronouns
topics.explanation: Spanish subject pronouns identify who performs the action. They are often omitted because the verb ending already identifies the subject.
rules: yo = I; tú = you informal singular; él = he; ella = she.
nosotros/nosotras = we; ellos/ellas = they.
usted = you formal singular; ustedes = you plural in Latin American Spanish.
Subject pronouns are used for emphasis, contrast or clarity, but are often unnecessary.

topics.title: Tú, usted and ustedes
topics.explanation: Latin American Spanish generally uses tú for informal singular 'you', usted for formal singular 'you', and ustedes for plural 'you'.
rules: tú uses second-person singular verb forms: tú tienes, tú hablas.
usted uses third-person singular verb forms: usted tiene, usted habla.
ustedes uses third-person plural verb forms: ustedes tienen, ustedes hablan.
Regional use of vos exists in parts of Latin America, but this reference uses standard tú forms.

topics.title: Ser
topics.explanation: Ser is used for identity, origin, profession, characteristics, dates, times and other relatively defining information.
rules: soy, eres, es, somos, son.
Use ser for identity: Soy Ana.
Use ser for origin: Soy de Perú.
Use ser for profession or status: Soy estudiante.
Use ser for characteristics: La casa es grande.
Use ser for dates, days and clock time: Hoy es lunes. Son las tres.
Events are located with ser: La reunión es en la oficina.
examples: La reunión es en mi casa.

topics.title: Estar
topics.explanation: Estar is used mainly for location and current or temporary states.
rules: estoy, estás, está, estamos, están.
Use estar for location: Vivo en Lima. / Madrid está en España.
Use estar for current states: Estoy cansado.
Use estar for temporary conditions: La comida está caliente.
Do not use estar simply because something is temporary in English. Learn the common ser/estar patterns.

topics.title: Ser vs estar
topics.explanation: The basic A1 distinction is that ser identifies or characterises something, while estar usually locates something or describes a current state.
rules: ser: identity, origin, profession, characteristics, dates, time and events.
estar: location and current states.
The contrast can change the meaning: Juan es aburrido = Juan is boring; Juan está aburrido = Juan is bored.
Some adjectives can be used with either verb with different meanings. At A1, learn the most common contrasts rather than trying to memorise every possibility.

topics.title: Present tense: regular -ar verbs
topics.explanation: Regular -ar verbs use predictable present-tense endings.
rules: Remove -ar and add: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -an.
yo hablo; tú hablas; él/ella/usted habla; nosotros hablamos; ellos/ellas/ustedes hablan.
Spanish often omits the subject pronoun because the ending identifies the person.

topics.title: Present tense: regular -er and -ir verbs
topics.explanation: Regular -er and -ir verbs have predictable present-tense endings.
rules: -er: -o, -es, -e, -emos, -en.
-ir: -o, -es, -e, -imos, -en.
Compare: comer → como, comes, come, comemos, comen.
Compare: vivir → vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, viven.

topics.title: Stem-changing verbs
topics.explanation: Many common present-tense verbs change a vowel in the stem in most forms. The nosotros/nosotras form usually keeps the original stem vowel.
rules: e → ie: pensar → pienso, piensas, piensa, pensamos, piensan.
o → ue: poder → puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, pueden.
e → i: pedir → pido, pides, pide, pedimos, piden.
The ending still follows the verb's -ar, -er or -ir pattern.

topics.title: Common irregular present verbs
topics.explanation: Some very common verbs have irregular forms that must be learnt individually or by pattern.
rules: ir: voy, vas, va, vamos, van.
tener: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen.
hacer: hago, haces, hace, hacemos, hacen.
decir: digo, dices, dice, decimos, dicen.
poner: pongo, pones, pone, ponemos, ponen.
venir: vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, vienen.
dar: doy, das, da, damos, dan.
ver: veo, ves, ve, vemos, ven.
saber: sé, sabes, sabe, sabemos, saben.

topics.title: Negation
topics.explanation: The basic negative word is no. It normally comes directly before the conjugated verb.
rules: no + verb: No hablo español.
With a second negative word, Spanish commonly uses no before the verb: No veo nada.
Common negative words include nada, nadie, nunca and ningún/ninguna.
Negative words can also occur without no when they come before the verb: Nadie viene.

topics.title: Questions and question words
topics.explanation: Spanish questions are marked with an opening ¿ and a closing ?. Question words normally carry an accent when they are interrogative.
rules: qué = what; quién/quiénes = who; dónde = where; cuándo = when.
cómo = how; por qué = why; cuánto/cuánta/cuántos/cuántas = how much/many.
Cuál/cuáles can mean which/what when selecting or identifying.
Question word order is flexible, but the question word normally comes near the beginning.

topics.title: Basic prepositions
topics.explanation: Prepositions connect words and show relationships such as location, movement, origin, company, purpose and time.
rules: a = to/towards; en = in/on/at; de = from/of; con = with; sin = without.
para commonly expresses purpose, destination or recipient.
por has several meanings, including through, around and because of, and is also used in expressions such as por la mañana.
hacia means towards; entre means between; sobre can mean on/about; contra means against.

topics.title: Al and del
topics.explanation: The prepositions a and de contract with the definite article el.
rules: a + el → al.
de + el → del.
No contraction occurs with la, los or las.
These contractions are obligatory in standard Spanish.

topics.title: Hay
topics.explanation: Hay means there is or there are. It describes the existence or presence of something rather than locating a specific known thing.
rules: Hay works with singular and plural nouns: hay un banco, hay dos bancos.
Negative: no hay.
Questions: ¿Hay un supermercado cerca?
Compare hay with estar: Hay un banco aquí. El banco está aquí.

topics.title: Possessive adjectives
topics.explanation: Possessive adjectives show who something belongs to. They agree with the thing possessed in number, and nuestro forms also agree in gender.
rules: yo: mi/mis; tú: tu/tus; él/ella/usted: su/sus.
nosotros: nuestro/nuestra/nuestros/nuestras.
ustedes/ellos/ellas: su/sus.
Possessives normally come before the noun.

topics.title: Demonstratives
topics.explanation: Demonstratives point to things according to their distance from the speaker.
rules: este/esta/estos/estas = this/these, generally near the speaker.
ese/esa/esos/esas = that/those, generally farther away or associated with the listener.
esto/eso can refer to an unspecified thing.
Demonstratives agree with the noun in gender and number.

topics.title: Gustar and similar structures
topics.explanation: Gustar works differently from English 'like'. The thing liked is grammatically the subject, and the person who likes it is represented by an indirect object pronoun.
rules: me gusta + singular noun or infinitive.
me gustan + plural noun.
Pronouns: me, te, le, nos, les.
To clarify or contrast the person, use a + person: A Ana le gusta el café.
Other common verbs follow a similar pattern: encantar, interesar and faltar.
examples: A Ana le gusta la música.

topics.title: Reflexive verbs
topics.explanation: Reflexive verbs describe actions that the subject performs on themselves or routines associated with the subject.
rules: Reflexive pronouns: me, te, se, nos, se.
The pronoun normally comes before a conjugated verb: me levanto.
Common A1 reflexive verbs include llamarse, levantarse, ducharse, acostarse, despertarse and sentirse.
With an infinitive, the pronoun can attach to the infinitive: voy a levantarme.

topics.title: Numbers
topics.explanation: Numbers are used for age, prices, quantities, addresses, dates and times.
rules: Learn at least 0–100 at A1.
Age uses tener: Tengo veinte años.
Uno changes to un before a masculine singular noun and una before a feminine singular noun: un libro, una casa.
Numbers normally come before the noun: tres libros.

topics.title: Time and dates
topics.explanation: Spanish uses ser for clock time and dates. Clock times normally use es la for one and son las for other hours.
rules: Es la una. Son las dos.
Use a la una and a las dos when giving the time of an event.
Days: lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo.
Months: enero, febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto, septiembre, octubre, noviembre, diciembre.
Specific dates use el: el 10 de agosto.
Repeated weekdays can use los: trabajo los lunes.
examples: La clase es a las tres.
Mi cumpleaños es el 10 de agosto.

topics.title: Nationalities and origin adjectives
topics.explanation: Nationalities are adjectives and therefore agree with the person or noun they describe.
rules: Use ser for nationality: Soy mexicano.
Many nationalities have masculine/feminine forms: mexicano/mexicana.
Plural forms also agree: mexicanos/mexicanas.
Origin can also be expressed with de + country: Soy de México.

topics.title: De for possession and description
topics.explanation: De commonly connects a thing with its owner, origin, material, contents or description.
rules: Possession: el libro de María.
Origin: una persona de Perú.
Contents/type: una taza de café.
Description or association: la capital de México.
De + el contracts to del.

topics.title: Ir a + infinitive
topics.explanation: Ir a + infinitive is the common A1 way to talk about a planned or imminent future action.
rules: Conjugate ir, then add a + infinitive.
voy a, vas a, va a, vamos a, van a.
The second verb remains in the infinitive.

topics.title: Tener que + infinitive
topics.explanation: Tener que + infinitive expresses obligation or something that must be done.
rules: Conjugate tener and add que + infinitive.
tengo que, tienes que, tiene que, tenemos que, tienen que.
The second verb remains in the infinitive.

topics.title: Modal verbs + infinitive
topics.explanation: Common modal verbs such as poder, querer and deber can be followed by an infinitive to express ability, desire or obligation.
rules: poder + infinitive = can/be able to.
querer + infinitive = want to.
deber + infinitive = should/must.
The modal is conjugated; the following verb stays in the infinitive.

topics.title: Estar + gerund
topics.explanation: Estar + gerund describes an action that is happening or in progress around a particular moment.
rules: -ar verbs form the gerund with -ando: hablar → hablando.
-er/-ir verbs normally form it with -iendo: comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo.
Some common forms are irregular: leer → leyendo, hacer → haciendo.
Use estar + gerund: Estoy trabajando.

topics.title: Weather expressions
topics.explanation: Spanish commonly uses fixed expressions rather than translating English weather sentences word for word.
rules: hace calor/frío = it is hot/cold.
hace sol = it is sunny; hace viento = it is windy.
hay niebla = it is foggy / there is fog.
llueve = it rains/is raining; nieva = it snows.
está lloviendo = it is raining right now.

topics.title: Muy and mucho
topics.explanation: Muy normally modifies adjectives or adverbs. Mucho expresses a large quantity or amount and agrees with nouns when it is an adjective.
rules: muy + adjective/adverb: muy grande, muy bien.
mucho/mucha/muchos/muchas + noun: mucho tiempo, muchas personas.
Mucho can follow a verb: Trabajo mucho.
Do not use muy directly before a noun.

topics.title: Más and menos
topics.explanation: Más means more and menos means less or fewer. They can modify nouns, adjectives, adverbs or verbs.
rules: más/menos + noun: más tiempo, menos dinero.
más/menos + adjective: más grande, menos caro.
más/menos + verb: trabajo más, duermo menos.
With a comparison, use más/menos + adjective + que.

topics.title: Basic comparisons
topics.explanation: Basic comparisons use más or menos + adjective/adverb + que.
rules: más ... que = more ... than.
menos ... que = less ... than.
más/menos + noun + que can compare quantities.
Common fixed comparison: mejor = better, peor = worse.
examples: Es más grande que mi casa.

topics.title: Cada
topics.explanation: Cada means each or every and is followed by a singular noun.
rules: cada + singular noun: cada día, cada semana.
Cada does not change for gender or number.
It often describes repeated routines.

topics.title: Basic frequency expressions
topics.explanation: Common frequency expressions describe how often something happens.
rules: siempre = always; normalmente = normally; a veces = sometimes; nunca = never.
These can usually be placed before the verb or in another natural position depending on the expression.
Nunca can make the sentence negative without no when it comes before the verb.

topics.title: Basic spatial prepositions
topics.explanation: A few additional prepositions are useful for describing simple locations and movement.
rules: sobre = on/about; entre = between; hacia = towards; contra = against.
Prepositions are normally followed by a noun or pronoun phrase.
examples: El libro está sobre la mesa.
Está entre la farmacia y el hotel.
La bicicleta está contra la pared.

topics.title: Common accent pairs: tú/tu and él/el
topics.explanation: Written accents can distinguish words that otherwise look identical.
rules: tú = you; tu = your.
él = he; el = the.
qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo, quién and cuánto take accents when used as question words.
Accents can change meaning, so learners should treat them as part of the word.

topics.title: Basic Spanish sentence structure
topics.explanation: Spanish commonly follows subject + verb + object, but word order is flexible because verb endings carry information.
rules: Basic statement: María vive en Lima.
Subject pronouns can be omitted: Vivo en Lima.
Adjectives commonly follow nouns: una casa grande.
Negation places no before the conjugated verb.
Questions can change word order or rely mainly on intonation and question words.

topics.title: Question formation
topics.explanation: Spanish does not require the same subject-verb inversion as English. A statement can become a question through punctuation, intonation or a question word.
rules: ¿Vives en Lima? can correspond to 'Do you live in Lima?'
¿Dónde vives? uses the question word plus the verb.
Subject pronouns can be retained for clarity or emphasis: ¿Tú vives aquí?
Use opening and closing question marks in writing.

topics.title: Common gerund spelling patterns
topics.explanation: Most gerunds are regular, but a few high-frequency verbs have forms worth learning early.
rules: -ar → -ando: hablar → hablando.
-er/-ir → -iendo: comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo.
Verbs such as leer use -yendo: leyendo.
Hacer has haciendo.

topics.title: Prepositions with time
topics.explanation: Spanish uses a small set of predictable prepositions in common time expressions.
rules: a + clock time: a las ocho.
en + month/year: en mayo, en 2026.
por + parts of the day: por la mañana, por la tarde.
de + time range/period in common expressions: de lunes a viernes.

topics.title: Basic object pronouns in fixed expressions
topics.explanation: A1 learners encounter a few very common object-pronoun patterns. These are best learnt as short structures rather than as a complete advanced pronoun system.
rules: me, te, lo/la, nos and los/las can represent the person or thing affected by an action.
In simple sentences the pronoun normally comes before a conjugated verb: Me llamo Ana.
With gustar, me/te/le/nos/les identifies the person experiencing the feeling.
Do not try to master every object-pronoun distinction at A1.

topics.title: Contractions and fixed combinations
topics.explanation: Spanish has a small number of common combinations that should be learnt as fixed forms.
rules: a + el = al; de + el = del.
Some preposition phrases are conventional: por la mañana, a las tres, de lunes a viernes.
Do not create contractions with la, los or las.

topics.title: Infinitives after common verbs
topics.explanation: After many common verbs, a second verb remains in the infinitive. The first verb carries the tense and person.
rules: quiero + infinitive: Quiero comer.
puedo + infinitive: Puedo ayudar.
debo + infinitive: Debo estudiar.
voy a + infinitive: Voy a viajar.
tengo que + infinitive: Tengo que trabajar.

topics.title: A1 grammar checklist
topics.explanation: At the end of A1, a learner should be able to recognise and use the core structures needed for simple everyday communication.
rules: Identify gender and number and make basic noun/adjective agreement.
Use articles, possessives and demonstratives.
Use subject pronouns appropriately and understand tú, usted and ustedes.
Conjugate common regular and high-frequency irregular present-tense verbs.
Use ser, estar and hay in their main A1 functions.
Form basic questions and negatives.
Use common prepositions, including al and del.
Express likes with gustar and basic routines with reflexive verbs.
Talk about numbers, age, prices, dates and times.
Talk about simple future plans with ir a + infinitive and obligations with tener que + infinitive.
Recognise basic stem-changing verbs and common progressive forms.
Describe weather, quantity, frequency and simple comparisons.
